themes.name: Prompt engineering
themes.description: Studies evaluating the impact of prompt design and optimization on LLM screening accuracy and sensitivity.

themes.name: Model performance comparisons
themes.description: Direct comparisons of different large language models (e.g., GPT‑4, Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT) for title/abstract screening accuracy.

themes.name: Efficiency and workload reduction
themes.description: Evidence on time savings, processing speed, and reduction of human workload when using LLMs for screening.

themes.name: LLM versus supervised machine learning
themes.description: Comparative evaluations of LLMs against traditional supervised machine‑learning classifiers for title‑abstract screening.

Prompt engineering.narrative: Optimised prompt templates for GPT‑4‑0125‑preview yielded very high abstract‑screening sensitivity (97.7%, 95% CI 86.7–100) and moderate specificity (85.2%, 95% CI 68.3–95.9) across 48 425 citations from ten systematic reviews, whereas zero‑shot prompts performed poorly (sensitivity ≈49%) [R0006]. In a prospective diagnostic study of GPT‑4‑Turbo, the initial prompt achieved a sensitivity of 0.75 (95% CI 0.43–0.92) and specificity of 0.99 (95% CI 0.99–0.99); post‑hoc prompt modifications increased sensitivity to 0.91 (95% CI 0.77–0.97) but reduced specificity slightly to 0.98 (95% CI 0.96–0.99) [R0028]. Homiar et al. reported that refined prompts for GPT‑4o reached 100% sensitivity for ultimately included studies, though sensitivity across updates varied between 58% and 100% and precision remained low (4–20%), indicating that prompt engineering can guarantee recall at the cost of many false positives [R0089]. Qiu et al. demonstrated that structured, prompt‑based workflows allowed ChatGPT to achieve 98–100% sensitivity and 80.6–93% specificity across three datasets, with full‑text screening requiring human correction of residual false positives [R0064]. Sanghera et al. showed that on a balanced development set of 800 records, optimal prompts gave perfect sensitivity (1.00) and high precision (0.927), but on a large, imbalanced dataset (119 695 records) precision fell dramatically (0.004–0.096) despite maintaining sensitivity up to 1.00, highlighting the influence of prompt bias and class imbalance on performance [R0057]. Across studies, higher sensitivity consistently accompanies more elaborate, task‑specific prompts, while specificity and precision are more variable and often lower, especially when datasets are large or unbalanced.
Prompt engineering.certainty_rationale: Evidence is observational with some concerns for bias and inconsistency across prompt designs and datasets, leading to downgrades for risk of bias and inconsistency.

Model performance comparisons.narrative: Across five diagnostic accuracy studies, large language models (LLMs) showed variable performance for title and abstract screening. Insuk et al. reported that human reviewers achieved the highest accuracy (0.9593) followed by Claude (0.9448) and ChatGPT (0.9138) [R0039]. Oami et al. found GPT‑4o to have high specificity (0.98) but lower sensitivity (0.75), whereas Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved higher sensitivities (0.93 and 0.95) at the cost of lower specificities (0.86 and 0.81) [R0040]. Sood et al. observed Gemini Flash 1.5 attaining the greatest overall accuracy (96.02%) while GPT‑4 showed the highest sensitivity (95.97%) and comparable agreement with humans (88.77%) [R0052]. Fazeli et al. reported GPT‑4o mini’s accuracy of 85.1% with sensitivity 83.2% and specificity 85.2% on a large record set (n=15,605) [R0053]. Zhan et al. demonstrated Review Copilot reaching sensitivity 99.2% and specificity 83.6% across four reviews, albeit with limited sample detail [R0070]. Kwok et al. noted commercial LLMs (ChatGPT, Copilot) achieving similar accuracy (83%–86%) and recall (87%–88%) to local implementations, while traditional NLP methods outperformed them [R0048]. Overall, models that prioritize sensitivity (Gemini, Claude) tend to miss fewer relevant studies but include more false positives, whereas models emphasizing specificity (GPT‑4o, Llama 3.3) reduce false positives but may exclude relevant records. Differences likely stem from prompting strategies, sample sizes, and reference‑standard definitions, with several studies relying on abstracts only and showing unclear risk of bias.
Model performance comparisons.certainty_rationale: Evidence is downgraded for risk of bias (unclear or some concerns), inconsistency across models, indirectness of reference standards, and imprecision due to small or unreported sample sizes.

Efficiency and workload reduction.narrative: Across five investigations, LLMs consistently reduced screening workload compared with human reviewers. Oami et al. reported that processing 100 studies fell from 17.2 minutes to 1.3 minutes, a mean saving of 15.25 minutes per 100 records [R0028]. Kwok et al. found that commercial LLMs cut total screening time to 37% of that required by humans, equating to roughly a three‑fold speedup [R0048]. Li et al. observed that their LLM tools required only 10–20 minutes to process 200 abstracts, indicating high time efficiency relative to manual duplicate screening [R0074]. Qiu et al. demonstrated that a structured prompt‑based workflow enabled screening of 3,821 abstracts and 261 full texts without programming, though human oversight remained necessary for false‑positive correction [R0064]. Zhan et al. reported that Review Copilot completed title/abstract screening in one‑quarter of human time and could exclude 90–95% of irrelevant articles at a rate of 1,000 articles per four person‑hours [R0070]. While all studies show substantial time savings, the magnitude varies with LLM version, prompting strategy, and dataset size, and some reports rely on abstracts only or have limited sample description, introducing uncertainty about generalisability.
Efficiency and workload reduction.certainty_rationale: Evidence is downgraded for risk of bias (unblinded designs, limited reporting) and inconsistency in reporting metrics and sample sizes, but remains moderate due to consistent direction of effect across multiple studies.

LLM versus supervised machine learning.narrative: A comparative evaluation was conducted using six open‑source systematic review datasets to benchmark a zero‑shot Llama‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct large language model (LLM) against four traditional supervised machine‑learning (SML) classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Naïve Bayes) for title‑abstract screening [R0042]. The LLM achieved recall values that were described as close to or above those of human reviewers, indicating comparable sensitivity to expert screening [R0042]. In contrast, the SML models demonstrated higher specificity than human reviewers but fell short of human recall, suggesting a trade‑off between false‑positive reduction and missed inclusions [R0042]. Naïve Bayes performed worse in recall yet exceeded human recall on average, highlighting variability among SML approaches [R0042]. Performance varied markedly across the six datasets, reflecting dataset‑specific influences on model accuracy and limiting the generalisability of any single metric [R0042]. The study provided bootstrap‑based confidence intervals for all reported measures, but the reliance on retrospectively labelled human decisions introduces potential misclassification bias and limits external validity [R0042]. Overall, the evidence suggests that LLMs can match human recall while SML classifiers may offer higher specificity, though results are heterogeneous across contexts [R0042].
LLM versus supervised machine learning.certainty_rationale: Observational design with some concerns of bias, high inconsistency across datasets, and indirectness due to reliance on retrospective human labels.

discussion.summary_of_evidence: The evidence from 13 studies indicates that large language models (LLMs) can achieve very high sensitivity for title and abstract screening when prompts are carefully engineered, with reported sensitivities ranging from 75% to 100% and specificities from 81% to 99% [R0006,R0028,R0089,R0064,R0057]. Prompt optimisation consistently improves recall but often reduces precision, especially on large, imbalanced datasets. Direct model comparisons show variable accuracy: some LLMs (e.g., Gemini, Claude) prioritize sensitivity, while others (e.g., GPT‑4o) achieve higher specificity, leading to trade‑offs between missed inclusions and false positives [R0039,R0040,R0052,R0053,R0070,R0048]. Efficiency outcomes are more uniform, with LLMs reducing screening time by roughly two‑ to three‑fold compared with human reviewers across several investigations [R0028,R0048,R0074,R0064,R0070]. When benchmarked against traditional supervised machine‑learning classifiers, LLMs match or exceed human recall but often have lower specificity, whereas SML models tend to be more precise but miss more relevant records [R0042]. Overall, the moderate certainty evidence supports that LLMs can reliably identify relevant studies if recall is prioritised, though precision and workload savings vary with prompt design and dataset characteristics.
discussion.limitations_of_evidence: Most studies have some concerns for bias, including unblinded designs, reliance on abstract‑only data, and unclear reference standards, which downgrade confidence [R0006,R0028,R0042]. Heterogeneity in prompt engineering, model versions, and dataset composition leads to inconsistency across reported sensitivities and specificities. Sample sizes are often small or poorly described, limiting precision of effect estimates, and several investigations lack external validation, reducing generalisability. Comparative studies frequently use retrospective human decisions as the gold standard, introducing potential misclassification bias.
discussion.implications: Practitioners can consider LLMs as a rapid screening adjunct, especially when high recall is essential, but should anticipate substantial false‑positive rates and retain human oversight for final inclusion decisions. Future research should standardise prompt frameworks, evaluate performance on diverse, fully‑text datasets, and conduct prospective, blinded trials to clarify accuracy and efficiency. Comparative studies with supervised machine‑learning methods should explore hybrid approaches that combine LLM recall with SML precision to optimise both sensitivity and workload reduction.

rationale: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a potential solution to the labor‑intensive title‑and‑abstract screening stage that delays systematic reviews, yet their reliability compared with expert human reviewers remains unclear [R0108]. Early investigations report promising accuracy for GPT‑4o and related models, but also highlight the need for higher precision to meet the standards required for clinical and policy‑making evidence [R0089, R0053]. Empirical evaluations across diverse domains—including radiology, venture‑capital evidence synthesis, and general biomedical literature—show that LLMs can achieve sensitivities and specificities approaching those of human reviewers, but performance varies with prompt design, model size, and the presence of disagreement, underscoring the importance of careful human‑in‑the‑loop oversight [R0073, R0006, R0082]. Comparative work suggests that zero‑shot, criteria‑prompted LLMs can match or exceed supervised machine‑learning baselines, yet the evidence is fragmented, with most studies focusing on single model families or specific review topics, and limited data on ensemble approaches or broader applicability [R0042, R0025]. Consequently, a systematic synthesis of existing empirical assessments is needed to clarify the accuracy of LLM‑driven screening, identify conditions under which they can reliably augment or replace human judgment, and guide methodological recommendations for future systematic review workflows.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "Oami et al. observed a rise in sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 after post‑hoc prompt modifications while maintaining high specificity (0.98) for GPT‑4 Turbo, indicating that prompt refinement can boost recall without sacrificing precision [R0028]." — The evidence states that specificity decreased from 0.99 to 0.98 after the prompt modifications. The draft claims specificity was 'maintained' and that precision was not sacrificed, which contradicts the reported drop in specificity.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change the description to note that specificity decreased slightly from 0.99 to 0.98, or remove the claim that precision was not sacrificed.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "The LLM achieved a recall of 0.86, which was comparable to or higher than the recall reported for human reviewers" — The evidence states that the LLM achieved recall values 'close to or above' human reviewers, but does not provide a specific aggregate recall value of 0.86 for the LLM. The value 0.86 appears in the 'Effects' section of the evidence card labeled as 'Recall: accuracy = 0.86', which is ambiguous and likely refers to a different metric or a specific dataset not explicitly linked to the LLM's overall performance in the text. Furthermore, the text says SML models 'exceeded human specificity while falling behind human recall', but the draft claims the LLM's recall was 'comparable to or higher', which is supported, but the specific number 0.86 is not explicitly attributed to the LLM's overall recall in the supporting passages.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Remove the specific number 0.86 or verify if it is the correct aggregate recall for the LLM. The text supports that the LLM's recall was close to or above human reviewers, but the specific value 0.86 is not clearly supported as the LLM's overall recall in the provided passages.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "Specificity for the LLM was 0.79, falling between the higher specificity of the SML models and the lower specificity of human screening." — The evidence states that SML models 'exceeded human specificity'. It does not state that the LLM's specificity (0.79) fell *between* the SML models and human reviewers. The evidence only says SML exceeded human specificity. It does not compare the LLM's specificity to the SML models' specificity or place it in a specific order relative to both. The claim that it falls 'between' is an unsupported inference.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Remove the claim that the LLM's specificity fell between the SML models and human reviewers. State only that the LLM's specificity was 0.79 and that SML models exceeded human specificity, without ranking the LLM's specificity relative to the SML models unless explicitly stated.

revision_issues.description: "Five studies demonstrated workload reductions of 60–75 %" — The thematic synthesis states that Kwok et al. found LLMs cut screening time to 37% of human time (a 63% reduction) and Zhan et al. reported completion in one-quarter of human time (a 75% reduction). However, the synthesis does not provide specific percentage reductions for the other three studies (Oami, Li, Qiu), only noting 'substantial time savings' or specific minute savings. The abstract's claim of a consistent 60-75% range across all five studies is not supported by the provided synthesis text, which lacks the data to verify the lower bound for the other studies.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Revise the abstract to state that studies reported substantial time savings, with specific examples of 63-75% reductions (or 'up to 75%'), or verify the specific percentages for all five studies against the full source data before asserting a uniform range.

revision_issues.description: "Further high‑quality, standardized evaluations are needed before routine replacement of human screening." — The thematic synthesis concludes that 'no single model consistently outperforms others' and notes 'low to moderate certainty' evidence. It does not support the conclusion that LLMs are ready for 'routine replacement' of human screening, nor does it suggest that replacement is a viable near-term outcome. The synthesis emphasizes the need for human oversight due to false positives and the trade-off between sensitivity and precision. The phrase 'before routine replacement' implies a trajectory toward replacement that is not substantiated by the current evidence, which highlights persistent limitations and the necessity of human oversight.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change the conclusion to reflect that LLMs are useful adjuncts to human screening, and that further research is needed to determine their role in augmenting (rather than replacing) human workflows, or to establish conditions under which they can be safely integrated with human oversight.
